title: Supernova 1987A Debris Disk
caption: Supernova 1987A and its ring of debris, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
credit: NASA, ESA, and P. Challis (Harvard-Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics)

recognition.text: NASA Hubble image release (STScI). No published audience rating.

story: A ring of supernova debris glows in this Hubble Space Telescope image of SN 1987A, which lies in the Large Magellanic Cloud, a neighboring galaxy. Light from the exploding star reached Earth in February 1987, making it the closest supernova seen from Earth in almost 400 years.

Because it is so near, astronomers have been able to follow the explosion in detail as it changes. Hubble has kept a continuous record of SN 1987A since the telescope's launch in 1990, as part of a long-term study led by Robert Kirshner of the Harvard-Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics.

For years the debris faded, but it has started to brighten again, which means a new power source is lighting it. The debris is beginning to strike the surrounding ring and drive powerful shock waves that produce X-rays, detected by NASA's Chandra X-ray Observatory. Those X-rays light up the debris, and shock heating makes it glow in visible light. NASA describes this as an unprecedented view of a supernova turning into a supernova remnant.

understand.summary: A Hubble Space Telescope image. NASA has not published the filters or color mapping for this image.
understand.eye: The colors are not documented, so they should not be read as the hues an eye would see, and the glow of the debris is lit partly by X-rays that the eye cannot see.

explore: The brightening was reported in the journal Nature by a team that included Kirshner. Hubble's long record of the object lets astronomers compare the debris over the years, which is how the change in the power source lighting the debris was noticed.
sources: NASA release: New Supernova Remnant Lights Up
alt: A brightening ring of supernova debris around the site of SN 1987A.
